Q: Fail remaining pytest tests if a specific one fails A:

You could try setting a global variable in a test and referencing it in a later test like so:

def test_check_connection(self):
    ...
    if Failed:
        global failed_conn_check = True
    else:
        global failed_conn_check = False

Then at the end of the tests:

    ...
    if failed_conn_check:
        raise SomeException
    ...

Q: Long-running 'py.test' stop at first failure A:

You can use addopts in the pytest.ini file. It does not require invoking any command line switch.

# Content of pytest.ini
[pytest]
addopts = --maxfail=2  # Exit after two failures

You can also set environment variable PYTEST_ADDOPTS before the test is run.

If you want to use Python code to exit after the first failure, you can use this code:

import pytest

@pytest.fixture(scope='function', autouse=True)
def exit_pytest_first_failure():
    if pytest.TestReport.outcome == 'failed':
        pytest.exit('Exiting pytest')

This code applies the exit_pytest_first_failure fixture to all test and exits pytest in case of a first failure.

Q: Differences between SQL dialects? A:

What you have listed are different products i.e. there are many relational databases out there which implement SQL, and they all implement it slightly differently. Thats where the dialects come from.

But you don't care (usually) about the SQL dialect when selecting a product, you care about a bunch of other factors, cost, reliability, scalability, performance etc etc

Q: How to remove [[nodiscard]] attribute from std::expected? A:

You wrote:

I know that ignoring std::expected is not a good practice [...]

Someone in the comments links to the /r/cpp discussion of MSVC's decision. Barry Revzin wrote at the time:

Yes. That's precisely why [std::expected] should be marked [[nodiscard]]. The only reason this type exists is to signal error [...]

And he's right. If you want something that behaves like expected<T,U> but doesn't have "error" semantics, you should reach for variant<T,U> instead. expected exists precisely to return "T or an error," and it is 100% incorrect to get an expected back from a function and then drop it on the floor without checking for that error. See "std::expected should be nodiscard" (December 2024):

Basically, in traditional exception-based error handling, you have these idiomatic lines:

return f();  // propagate both result and error
f();  // propagate error, discard result
try { f(); } catch (...) {}  // discard both

And in expected-based error handling, you have these:

return f();  // propagate both result and error
return f().and_then(~~~);  // propagate error, discard result
(void)f();  // discard both

Notice that “discard both” has a sigil in both cases: try { ~~ } catch(...){} in the former case and (void)~~ in the latter. But that’s just a style guideline at the moment; as long as expected isn’t marked [[nodiscard]] then it’s also legal to write just

f();  // discard both

which confusingly looks just like the “propagate error, discard result” line from the former exception-based case — and dangerously is possible to write without noticing. That’s the benefit of requiring the (void) sigil in order to discard a return value: the sigil increases the edit distance between the correct code and the incorrect code, while separating them with a spacious “no man’s land” of invalid code that will cause your build to fail.

But (because you already said "I know this isn't good practice") I know I'm preaching to the choir here. :)

I don't think there's a "quick fix" (again, this is pretty much by design), except to wrap the standard (nodiscard-by-design) std::expected in your own non-nodiscard class type my::expected (which can be a thin wrapper around std::expected); use my::expected everywhere; and then at some point in the future when your codebase is cleaner, replace my::expected with

namespace my { using std::expected; }

Q: Are these all the types of variadic arguments that printf() expects in MSVC? A:

Here is a stolen table from https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/io/fprintf

C printf Conversion Specifiers and Argument Types

Length Modifiers

Conversion Specifier Explanation hh h none l ll j z t L
% Writes literal % using %% N/A N/A N/A N/A N/A N/A N/A N/A N/A
c Writes a single character.
Without l: converted to unsigned char.
With l: treated as wchar_t[2].		 N/A N/A int wint_t N/A N/A N/A N/A N/A
s Writes a character string.
Without l: char*.
With l: wchar_t*, converted via wcrtomb.		 N/A N/A char* wchar_t* N/A N/A N/A N/A N/A
d, i Signed integer in decimal. signed char short int long long long intmax_t (signed size_t) ptrdiff_t N/A

u Unsigned decimal integer. unsigned char unsigned short unsigned int unsigned long unsigned long long uintmax_t size_t (unsigned ptrdiff_t) N/A
f, F Floating-point decimal. Default precision: 6. F uses uppercase. N/A N/A double double N/A N/A N/A N/A long double
e, E Floating-point in scientific notation. E uses uppercase. N/A N/A double double N/A N/A N/A N/A long double
a, A Floating-point in hexadecimal notation. A uses uppercase. N/A N/A double double N/A N/A N/A N/A long double
g, G Auto format float using e/f or E/F depending on value. N/A N/A double double N/A N/A N/A N/A long double

p Outputs an implementation-defined pointer representation. N/A N/A void* N/A N/A N/A N/A N/A N/A

Notes

  • The following specifiers are available since C99: hh, ll, j, z, t, F, a, A.
  • For char, short, unsigned char, unsigned short, default argument promotions apply (promoted to int or unsigned int).
  • Use macros in <inttypes.h> (like PRId8, PRIuMAX) for fixed-width types.
  • %n is security-sensitive and not allowed in printf_s (since C11).
  • Floating-point inf and nan results are implementation-defined (inf vs infinity, nan(...)).
  • Conversion behavior is undefined if the format is invalid.

Microsoft MSVC-Specific printf Format Specifiers

Format Specifier Type Notes
%I64d, %I64u, %I64x, %I64X __int64, unsigned __int64 Use instead of %lld / %llu
%I32d, %I32u __int32 Rarely used, equivalent to %d
%I16d, %I16u __int16 Rarely used, equivalent to %hd
%I8d, %I8u __int8 Rarely used, equivalent to %hhd
%Iu size_t Works on both x86 (32-bit) and x64 (64-bit)
%Id ptrdiff_t Platform-dependent width
%Ix / %IX uintptr_t / intptr_t Unsigned pointer-width integer
%hs char* (multibyte string) Same as %s in ANSI, but explicitly narrow in Unicode builds
%ls wchar_t* Wide string; use with Unicode
%S Depends on _UNICODE ANSI or Unicode string depending on build mode
%C Depends on _UNICODE Single character: char or wchar_t
%ws wchar_t* Always wide string, same as %ls
%wc wchar_t Always wide character
%T TCHAR (deprecated) Only if using <tchar.h> macros

Special Notes:

  • MSVC does not support C99’s %z, %j, %t in older versions (before Visual Studio 2015).
  • Use %Iu instead of C99’s %zu (for size_t).
  • Use PRId64, etc. from <inttypes.h> with Visual Studio 2013+, which added partial C99 support.
  • MSVC's printf_s disallows %n (like C11 bounds-checked printf).

Q: What's the industry-standard way to, with a formula, fill a range with a specific value? A:

You can use

=WRAPCOLS("Apple", 5, "Apple")

Or

=LET(s, "Apple", WRAPCOLS(s, 5, s))
